bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geopolitical conflict, sea-route closure and trade/tariff regimes hitting an export-heavy order book — The MD&A 'Threats' paragraph names the evolving geopolitical landscape, ongoing regional conflicts, supply chain disruptions and uncertainties from global trade policies and tariff regimes as challenges 'for manufacturers with significant export and import exposure', potentially affecting project execution timelines, material availability, logistics costs and overall operations. This is not theoretical for Anup: the MD & CEO records that in the last few weeks of FY26 critical materials 'not finding ways' and curtailed industrial gas supply restricted the pace of manufacturing, and that a sizeable accumulation of finished goods due to non-availability of shipping lines limited shop-floor flow and impacted progress of new work.
- Raw material price volatility (especially steel) and elevated input costs on long-cycle fixed-price orders — The MD & CEO cites volatility in raw material pricing especially steel, energy prices and higher logistics costs, and states the Company will be 'very judicious in booking new orders considering the current high input costs'. With average execution cycles of 12-14 months on large complex projects, input-cost movement between quotation and delivery is a structural margin risk; management also flags that labour, freight and royalty will remain relatively higher in the new order mix.
- Availability of skilled operators and technical personnel — Explicitly flagged in MD&A 'Threats': the business involves the design and manufacture of highly engineered, custom-built equipment, 'making the availability of a skilled workforce a critical success factor', and the industry continues to face challenges attracting and retaining skilled operators and technical personnel required to support growing demand. Mitigation stated is automation, digitalisation and productivity improvement plus workforce development.
- Execution risk and earnings lumpiness from large, complex, long-cycle projects — Management states that with the large-sized Kheda facility fully operational the Company is focused on taking large-sized complex projects with long execution cycles (average 12-14 months), so 'it is natural that you will see fluctuations in quarter-on-quarter numbers'. Execution slippage is already visible: the MD notes Mabel's contribution 'would have been better if not for some site projects which got prolonged than expected due to technical changes'. First-time entries into Nuclear, Thermal Power, Clean Energy Storage, Skids and Air Cooled Heat Exchangers add first-of-a-kind execution risk.
- Export concentration — BRSR item 19 discloses exports at 48.2% of total turnover in the reporting year, across 12 countries and 13 Indian states, and the MD states the export:domestic ratio continued at 50:50 as a matter of strategic intent. Roughly half of turnover is therefore exposed to cross-border logistics, tariff regimes, currency and the Middle East demand cycle that the MD&A identifies as the key export opportunity.
- Product and single-activity concentration — BRSR discloses one business activity - 'Fabrication of metal and metal products' - at 99.87% of turnover, and one product line (Heat Exchanger, Pressure Vessels, Towers, Reactors, Column and Centrifuges, NIC 28230) also at 99.87%. Within that, Shell & Tube Heat Exchangers have historically been approximately 70% of annual revenue, projected to moderate to approximately 60% in the current year - i.e. diversification is under way but concentration remains high.
- End-market cyclicality - dependence on process-industry capital expenditure — Demand is a derived function of capex by Oil & Gas, Petrochemicals, Fertilisers, Hydrogen, Power and LNG customers; MD&A explicitly grounds the outlook in 'healthy capital expenditure across key end-user industries' and 'significant greenfield and brownfield investments'. A capex pause in these industries, or a faster-than-expected transition away from Oil & Gas, transmits directly to order inflow.
- Worker safety exposure in a contract-labour-heavy fabrication workforce — BRSR Principle 3 reports 13 total recordable work-related injuries to workers in FY 2025-26 (6 in FY 2024-25) and one worker fatality in FY 2024-25 (none in FY 2025-26), while Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate is reported as 0 for both employees and workers in both years - an internal inconsistency worth noting. Of the 13 affected workers in FY26 and 6 in FY25, the number rehabilitated or placed in suitable employment is reported as 0. The workforce structure concentrates this risk: 0 permanent workers versus 783 other-than-permanent workers (100% male) against 391 permanent employees.
- Risk governance is framework-only, with no named enterprise risk register disclosed — The MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' section and the Directors' Report 'Risk Management Policy' section are near-identical boilerplate describing a Risk Management Committee of the Board, a Risk Management Policy, an Internal Audit Department facilitating identification/assessment/monitoring/mitigation, and annual Audit Committee review - but no specific risk is named, scored or quantified anywhere in either section. The BRSR material responsible-business-conduct issues table, which would normally carry the named risk/opportunity rows, is truncated in the routed material (only rows 7 Human Capital Management and 8 Diversity and Inclusion survive, both classified 'Opportunity').

outlook.body:
- Move up the value chain: capitalise on investments already made and shift to higher value-added products including design, critical & complex manufacturing and site services.
- Over the next 3 years, navigate to niche product segments that are proprietary in nature and complex in design.
- Treat FY27 as a year of Stabilisation, Strengthening fundamentals, Consolidation and Risk protection, with a clear focus on profits under current cost pressures and maintaining healthy cash flow; tread FY27 cautiously while preparing for the improved business expected thereafter.
- Be very judicious in booking new orders given current high input costs, even though order booking has improved and the enquiry pipeline is good.
- Focus on taking large-sized, complex projects with long execution cycles (average 12-14 months) now that the large-sized Kheda facility is fully operational, accepting quarter-on-quarter fluctuations that broadly normalise over the year.
- Foray into the Critical Equipment Business, evidenced by first orders in Nuclear, Thermal Power, Clean Energy Storage (for a European technology company), Skids and Air Cooled Heat Exchangers, and by delivery of the first Solid Inconel 200MT single-piece equipment to a Middle East client.
- Broaden the product portfolio away from dependence on Shell & Tube Heat Exchangers towards Reactors, Pressure Vessels, Columns & Towers and other large-scale fabricated equipment using the Kheda capability.
- Build the Technical Services business into a sizeable vertical (over 10 orders executed in FY26, dedicated organisation structure created), with capability spread across shop fabrication, site fabrication and technical services.
- Maintain the export:domestic ratio at around 50:50, described as being 'in line with our strategic intent'.
- Develop the Vadodara design office - now stabilised and supporting execution - into a profit contributor by taking external assignments.
- Counter the scarcity of skilled operators and technical personnel by enhancing automation, digitalisation and productivity across manufacturing facilities and business processes, while investing in workforce development and operational excellence.
- Integrate and leverage the Mabel Engineers acquisition to extend geographic presence into southern India and add Silos, Storage Tanks and Process Vessels to the portfolio.
- Stated policy intent rather than figures. The Board has adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy under Regulation 43A of the Listing Regulations, available on the Company's website, and for FY 2025-26 recommended a final dividend of Rs 12 per equity share of face value Rs 10, subject to shareholder approval at the 9th AGM (August 25, 2026), involving a cash outflow of approximately Rs 24.04 Crores. As permitted under the Companies Act, the Board does not propose to transfer any amount to general reserve. The Company has not accepted or renewed any deposits and has no outstanding deposits as at March 31, 2026. Members enhanced the borrowing limit under Section 180(1)(c) by special resolution at the AGM held on August 20, 2025 - a stated headroom decision, quantum not disclosed in this bundle. Equity issuance is being deliberately avoided: 5,000 equity shares were allotted on ESOP exercise during the year, and the ESOS 2019 has been moved to an irrevocable employee welfare trust that will acquire shares by secondary acquisition so there is 'no fresh issuance of equity shares and consequently no dilution of existing shareholding or impact on the Company's earnings per share'; no shares with differential voting rights and no sweat equity were issued. The Directors' Report states there are no material changes or commitments affecting the financial position between the end of the financial period and the date of the report. On reinvestment intent, the MD & CEO frames FY27 as consolidation - 'The focus shall be clearly on profits under the current cost pressures and maintain a healthy cash flow' - with the strategy being to sweat the capacity already created ('capitalise on the current investments made') rather than to announce new expansion. Governance-side remuneration policy: shareholders are being asked at the AGM to approve commission to Non-Executive Directors up to 1% of net profits for five years from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2031, with no single Non-Executive Director paid more than 50% of the total NED commission in a year without prior shareholder approval, and the cost auditor's FY 2026-27 remuneration of Rs 35,000 plus taxes is being ratified.
- Renewable electricity: the MD & CEO states that with rooftop solar at both Gujarat manufacturing facilities and a windmill, 'about 40% of our electricity requirement is met through renewables'. Annexure D discloses installed captive capacity of a 750 KW windmill and a 1790 KW solar plant, with generation set off against energy consumed in manufacturing units.
- Renewable generation mix moved sharply within FY26: solar generation rose to 17,87,341 units from 12,59,927 units, while windmill generation collapsed to 40,843 units from 2,76,328 units, out of total electricity used of 63,08,783 units (FY25: 55,44,428 units). The near-shutdown of the windmill is a material change the report does not explain.
- Green capex intensity: BRSR Principle 2 discloses 4.85% of capex in FY 2025-26 (0% in FY 2024-25) invested in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts; R&D investment in such technologies is 0% in both years, and the Company states it is 'yet to measure technology or innovation-wise environmental and social impact'.
- Occupational health & safety: an OH&S management system compliant with ISO 45001:2018 is implemented across all facilities and all Anup facilities are ISO 45001:2018 certified; a formal OHS Policy, dedicated qualified safety officers at each manufacturing unit, a health and safety committee with equal worker representation, HIRA for routine work and a Permit to Work system for non-routine work, On-Site Emergency Plans, annual ergonomic assessments, a Unified Reporting Tool and an anonymous Suggestion Box for hazard reporting are disclosed.
- Safety outcomes disclosed: 13 total recordable work-related injuries to workers in FY 2025-26 versus 6 in FY 2024-25; zero employee injuries; zero fatalities in FY 2025-26 versus one worker fatality in FY 2024-25; zero high-consequence injuries; LTIFR reported as 0 for both categories in both years (inconsistent with 13 recordable injuries and flagged as such); zero complaints on working conditions and on health & safety; 100% of plants and offices assessed for health & safety practices and working conditions; and 'There were no significant risk or concern arising from assessment of health & safety practices and working conditions'.
- Rehabilitation gap: of the 13 workers affected in FY 2025-26 and 6 in FY 2024-25, the number rehabilitated and placed in suitable employment (or whose family members were placed) is reported as 0 in both years - a stated nil that sits against an ISO 45001-certified safety posture.
- Workforce composition: 391 permanent employees (367 male, 24 female - 6.14% female) and zero other-than-permanent employees; zero permanent workers against 783 other-than-permanent workers, 100% male; 1 differently-abled permanent employee and 2 differently-abled other-than-permanent workers. Board of Directors 7 with 1 female (14.29%); Key Management Personnel 3 with 0 female (the count includes one Board member who is MD & CEO).
- Human-rights training coverage: 100% of permanent employees trained in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25 (391 and 309), while other-than-permanent workers went from 0% (0 of 737) in FY 2024-25 to 51.09% (400 of 783) in FY 2025-26 - improving but still leaving about half the contract workforce untrained.
- Performance and career development reviews slipped for employees: 90.80% of employees reviewed in FY 2025-26 (355 of 391) versus 100% in FY 2024-25 (309 of 309); workers remained at 100%.

- Anti-corruption and anti-bribery are covered within the Whistle-Blower Policy, published on the Company's website, alongside a grievance-redressal mechanism open to employees, workers, customers, investors, community members and value chain partners; investor grievances route to the Company Secretary and Compliance Officer.

outlook.body: Capacity build-out is the central operating story of FY 2025-26 and is described as essentially complete. Phase II of the expansion at the Kheda (Gujarat) manufacturing facility was successfully completed during the year, described in the MD&A as having 'enhanced production capacity, operational efficiency, and manufacturing flexibility'; the MD & CEO message quantifies it: 'We have completed our phase 2 expansion at Kheda increasing the capacity to 8000MT per year, with a revenue capacity of Rs 400 Cr to Rs 450 Cr.' The Kheda plant is described as new, strategically located close to the National Highway, and 'now fully operational', enabling manufacture of larger and heavier process equipment and a shift of mix towards Reactors, Pressure Vessels, Columns & Towers and other large-scale fabricated equipment. The second leg of the expansion was inorganic: Mabel Engineers Private Limited, the 100%-owned manufacturing subsidiary in Tamil Nadu (acquired June 19, 2024), had its operations successfully integrated and stabilised during FY26, adding southern-India geographic presence and Silos, Storage Tanks and Process Vessels to the portfolio. A design office at Vadodara has stabilised, supports execution and has recently started taking small external assignments. Taken together, the MD & CEO states that 'With these installed capacities at our 3 manufacturing locations, ie. Ahmedabad, Kheda and Mabel Engineers, we have a capacity capable of delivering revenue up to Rs 1200 Cr per year' - i.e. the stated posture for FY27 is to sweat capacity already created rather than to announce a new project; no new expansion project, commissioning date or capex quantum for a future project is disclosed anywhere in the routed bundle. Energy assets: a windmill of 750 KW capacity and a solar plant of 1790 KW capacity are installed, set off against energy consumed in manufacturing units (Annexure D, Conservation of Energy); the MD notes both Gujarat manufacturing facilities have rooftop solar and a windmill meeting about 40% of electricity requirement. BRSR Section A item 18 (standalone boundary) discloses only a location count - 2 plants and 1 office in India, none international - with no capacity figures; note this conflicts in appearance with the 3 manufacturing locations cited by the MD, because Mabel sits outside the standalone BRSR boundary. BRSR Principle 2 discloses that 4.85% of total capex investment in FY 2025-26 (0% in FY 2024-25) went into specific technologies improving environmental and social impacts, with R&D at 0% in both years - a percentage only, no rupee amount, and it is not a NAMED DISCLOSURE, so it is deliberately excluded from capex_disclosed. Annexure D also records that an amount was invested in energy-conservation equipment but the sentence is truncated mid-figure ('An amount of Rs 1' - text cut off), so that quantum is unusable. DEFECT NOTE on the NAMED DISCLOSURE block supplied for capital commitments: the same Note 27 appears twice, tagged [page 74] and [page 109], with identical figures 932.14 and 1,333.20. The page-74 header is truncated at 'As at' with no date at all; the page-109 header reads 'As at March 31, 2026'. Both headers also carry conflicting unit candidates - '(Rs in Lakhs) | (In Millions)' - although the note body itself states '(Rs in Lakhs)' twice, which is what has been used. Because only ONE column date is readable while TWO figures are printed, only the current-year figure has been emitted (932.14, as at 31 March 2026, matching the sole readable date and the customary first-column position); the second figure, 1,333.20, is the undated comparative and has been OMITTED rather than guessed. Verbatim reproduction of the block as supplied: '[page 74] (Rs in Lakhs) | (In Millions) | for the year ended March 31, 2026 | As at / Note 27 : Capital Commitment and Other Commitments / (Rs in Lakhs) / (a) Capital Commitments / (i) Estimated amount of Contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for (Net of advances) / 932.14 / 1,333.20' and '[page 109] (Rs in Lakhs) | (In Millions) | for the year ended March 31, 2026 | As at March 31, 2026 / Note 27 : Capital Commitment and Other Commitments / (Rs in Lakhs) / (a) Capital Commitments / (i) Estimated amount of Contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for (Net of advances) / 932.14 / 1,333.20'. Also note the page-74 tag is anomalous: per the annual report's own contents page, the Standalone Financial Statements begin at page 97, so a Note 27 appearing at page 74 falls inside the Corporate Governance Report page range - the duplicate is most likely the standalone/consolidated pair or a page-numbering artefact of the extractor, and it is flagged rather than resolved.

outlook.body:
- The Company expects sustained momentum in the domestic market in the coming quarters, underpinned by robust capital expenditure across core process industries.
- Continued development of natural gas infrastructure projects, particularly in the Middle East, is expected to provide attractive export opportunities and support future business growth.
- Healthy capital expenditure continues across key end-user industries - Petrochemicals, Natural Gas, Fertilisers, Hydrogen and Power - with significant greenfield and brownfield investment globally driven by energy security and self-sufficiency.
- Oil & Gas is expected to remain a critical part of the global energy mix even as the transition to a lower-carbon mix accelerates investment in clean energy.
- Increasing focus on green ammonia - for green fertilisers and as an enabler of the hydrogen economy - is expected to create substantial long-term opportunities for the process equipment industry.
- Accelerated global transition to cleaner energy (green hydrogen, green ammonia, carbon capture, renewables) is anticipated to generate substantial process-equipment demand, particularly in developed economies.
- Thermal power investments are gaining momentum across several Asian economies; thermal power projects 'which were written off are back strongly, with over 14GW in India for NTPC and other private conglomerates'.
- Growing focus on nuclear energy - conventional and small modular reactors - creates additional opportunity; the Company states it is part of the Kaiga 5 & 6 project under the NPCIL fleet programme to add 7GW to the national grid.
- Petrochemicals is seeing good growth globally, driven by demand in ethylene, propylene and specialty chemicals for packaging and consumer products; fertiliser is gaining traction in India, China and Africa (over 6 trains of fertiliser projects in Africa); LNG projects are in demand especially in the Middle East; refinery expansions, LNG, and large PTA, PVC & VCM projects in India.
- As geopolitical conditions stabilise in conflict-affected regions, significant opportunities are expected in the Middle East for repair, replacement and capacity enhancement, especially in natural gas; management expects the disruption to lead to energy-security investment, repair work for damaged refineries, gas plants, tanks and pipelines, and an accelerated push to non-conventional energy.
- India is strengthening its position as a preferred global manufacturing hub for critical process equipment, presenting growth opportunities for domestic manufacturers.
- Encouraging demand continues across Thermal Power, Natural Gas and Fertiliser projects, expected to remain important growth drivers in the near to medium term.
- Product mix shift is the stated swing factor: Heat Exchangers historically about 70% of annual revenue are projected to moderate to about 60% in the current year as Reactors, Pressure Vessels and Columns & Towers grow from Kheda.
- Cost structure is expected to change with the shift to large, complex and proprietary orders - labour, freight and royalty remaining relatively higher - and these are stated to be built into estimation and pricing.
- Headwinds flagged in the narrative: geopolitics and wars, trade tariff positions, energy price impact, raw-material (especially steel) price volatility, closure of the main sea route raising logistics costs; in the last few weeks of FY26 critical materials did not arrive, industrial gas supply was curtailed restricting the pace of manufacturing, and finished goods accumulated because shipping lines were unavailable, limiting shop-floor flow.
- Skilled-workforce availability is called a critical success factor for designing and manufacturing highly engineered, custom-built equipment, with the industry facing challenges attracting and retaining skilled operators and technical personnel.
- Directors' Report, Performance Review: 'All time high opening Order Book of Rs 769 Crores as on March 31, 2026.'
- MD&A (g): 'Strong order pipeline of Rs 769 Crores to provide good execution visibility.'
- MD & CEO message: 'On the order book, we have a pending order book of approx. Rs 769 Cr to be executed based on the delivery plans.'
- LABEL INCONSISTENCY (flagged, not resolved): the same Rs 769 Cr figure is described three different ways in the same annual report - 'opening Order Book' (Directors' Report), 'order pipeline' (MD&A) and 'pending order book' (MD & CEO message). The as-of date is stated only once, as on March 31, 2026.
- 'Order booking has surely improved, and with a good enquiry pipeline, we see good business opportunities for this year and the next year. Having said that, we will be very judicious in booking new orders considering the current high input costs.'
- Order composition is shifting to large-sized complex projects with long execution cycles, average 12-14 months, which management says will cause quarter-on-quarter fluctuations that broadly normalise over the year.
- New order categories won for the first time in FY26: Nuclear, Thermal Power, Clean Energy Storage technology (European technology company), Skids, and Air Cooled Heat Exchangers.
- Technical Services: over 10 orders executed in FY26.

risks.note: Management states that with the large-sized Kheda facility fully operational the Company is focused on taking large-sized complex projects with long execution cycles (average 12-14 months), so 'it is natural that you will see fluctuations in quarter-on-quarter numbers'. Execution slippage is already visible: the MD notes Mabel's contribution 'would have been better if not for some site projects which got prolonged than expected due to technical changes'. risks.note: BRSR item 19 discloses exports at 48.2% of total turnover in the reporting year, across 12 countries and 13 Indian states, and the MD states the export:domestic ratio continued at 50:50 as a matter of strategic intent. meta.thesis: Anup Engineering is executing a strategic transformation from a domestic heat exchanger specialist to a diversified process equipment manufacturer with expanded capacity at Kheda, targeting higher-margin exotic metallurgy and export markets, despite near-term margin pressure from raw material spikes. The company is poised for 25%+ CAGR over 3 years, supported by a robust order book and a new facility designed for complex, high-value equipment.
